text: Workspaces trade isolation for convenience, and that trade is sometimes exactly backwards for what an environment needs. One configuration, several named state files, terraform.workspace driving naming and sizing — that's genuinely low overhead. But every workspace in that setup still shares the same backend, the same provider block, and almost always the same credentials, so there's no built-in way to say only one team can touch prod.

So the choice isn't workspaces versus some vaguely better practice — it's convenience versus isolation. Workspaces fit environments that are structurally identical and trusted to the same people. Separate directories fit environments that need a real boundary: a different team, a different approval gate, a different set of permissions, or configuration that's genuinely started to diverge rather than just scale up or down.

A directory-per-environment layout looks like envs/dev and envs/prod, each with its own backend.tf and its own main.tf calling the exact same shared module from Chapter 4. The module code never duplicates — only the backend configuration and the variable values per directory do. That's the real cost of this approach: more files to keep in sync by hand, with nothing enforcing that each directory calls the module correctly.

What that buys back is real isolation. prod's backend block can point at its own storage account, in its own resource group, with its own Azure RBAC role assignments — a completely different access policy than dev's backend. prod's deployment pipeline can require a distinct service principal and a manual approval step that dev's pipeline skips entirely, because the state itself lives somewhere dev credentials simply can't reach.

Many real projects end up using both: workspaces for short-lived, low-risk environments like a feature branch's preview deploy, and separate directories for the hard boundary between non-production and production. Lesson 19 picks up the other half of the environment story — not where state lives, but how the same module produces a small dev environment and a much larger prod one from different variable files.
